topic: How a Bitcoin block actually gets mined
hook: Bitcoin miners are playing the world's biggest guessing game.

scenes.narration: Miners bundle transactions into a block, then hash the block header with SHA-256 over and over, searching for a result below the network's target.
The first miner to find one broadcasts the block. Finding it is hard, but other nodes can check it cheaply.
That miner collects the block reward: newly issued bitcoin plus the transaction fees in the block.

topic: What the Bitcoin block reward is and how halvings change it
hook: Every four years, Bitcoin miners get a pay cut. On purpose.

scenes.narration: A miner's reward for a block is the subsidy of new bitcoin, plus the transaction fees.
Every 210,000 blocks, roughly four years, the subsidy is cut in half.
At the April 2024 halving it dropped to 3.125 bitcoin per block.

description_body: The block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks. Since April 2024 it has been 3.125 BTC per block.

topic: Myth: more miners make Bitcoin blocks faster
hook: Myth: more miners means faster Bitcoin blocks. Here's why it's wrong.

scenes.narration: People assume that if more miners join, blocks arrive faster.
Every 2,016 blocks, about two weeks, Bitcoin recalculates difficulty.
If blocks come too quickly, difficulty rises, so the average stays close to ten minutes.

topic: Myth: you can mine Bitcoin profitably with a gaming GPU
hook: Can your gaming PC mine Bitcoin? Not in any practical way.

scenes.narration: Many beginners think a gaming graphics card can mine Bitcoin.
Specialised chips called ASICs are far more efficient at SHA-256 than graphics cards or CPUs.
Mining Bitcoin with a GPU is not practical today, because ASICs are so much more efficient at the same job.

hook: Two miners, same hashrate, very different electricity bills.

scenes.narration: One terahash per second means one trillion hash attempts every second.
Efficiency is measured in watts per terahash. Lower means less electricity for the same work.
To judge any miner, look at hashrate and efficiency together.

description_body: Hashrate tells you how fast a miner is. Watts per terahash tells you what that speed costs in electricity.

topic: Why electricity costs and the Bitcoin price decide mining profitability
hook: Mining rewards come in bitcoin. The bills arrive in regular money.

scenes.narration: Miners are paid in bitcoin.
Electricity and hosting are paid in regular currency, and electricity is usually the biggest ongoing cost.
So a falling bitcoin price or a rising power price can squeeze mining returns. Results vary, and they are never certain.

scenes.narration: Per a third-party explainer, owners are credited bitcoin rewards each day.
A maintenance charge covering electricity and service costs is deducted from those rewards.
Bitcoin's price and network difficulty change, so the net result can be low or even negative. And digital miners can't be redeemed for bitcoin.

topic: Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million
hook: There will only ever be 21 million bitcoin.

scenes.narration: Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins.
New coins enter circulation as block rewards paid to miners.
Because the reward halves every 210,000 blocks, new supply slows over time.

topic: Why Bitcoin proof of work is hard to fake
hook: Bitcoin mining is hard to do, but easy to check.

scenes.narration: Finding a block means searching for a header hash below the target. There's no shortcut except more guesses.
Once a block is found, other nodes can check its proof of work cheaply.
Honest checking is cheap, while cheating would take enormous computing work.

topic: Solo mining versus mining pools explained
hook: Solo mining versus a pool: what's the difference?

scenes.narration: Your chance of finding a block is your share of the network's total hashrate.
Solo miners can wait a long time between rewards, then get a whole block at once.
Pools combine hashrate and share rewards in proportion to the work each member contributed.
